title: GI & Nutrition Pharmacology — Session 2

summary.text: Laxatives fall into four buckets — **bulk-forming** (slowest, safest), **osmotic** (fast; PEG first-line), **stimulant** (short-term), **secretagogue** (IBS-C) — and osmotic/stimulant act in hours, bulk-forming in days.
**Loperamide** and **diphenoxylate/atropine** slow the gut via mu receptors; never use them in **C. difficile** or bloody/febrile diarrhea, and atropine is there to deter misuse.
IBD therapy **steps up with severity**: 5-ASA → short-term steroids → thiopurines for maintenance (test TPMT/NUDT15; cut dose with allopurinol) → biologics/small molecules.
Biologics share **immunosuppression risk**: screen TB and hepatitis B/C and update vaccines first; **vedolizumab** is the gut-selective one.
**Fat-soluble** vitamins (A, D, E, K) accumulate; water-soluble are excreted. Long-term **PPI or metformin** → check **B12**; refeed slowly with thiamine.

Warfarin’s effect falls with **dietary vitamin K** (pharmacodynamic) and with **St. John’s wort** (CYP3A4 induction, pharmacokinetic); ginkgo and fish oil raise bleeding — always ask about supplements.

chunks.text: **Opposite problems, each with its own family of mechanisms.** Four laxative buckets: bulk-forming, osmotic, stimulant, secretagogue — sort any laxative name into one of them.
**Bulk-forming** (psyllium, methylcellulose): absorb water, increase stool bulk and transit; slowest onset; generally safest for long-term use.
**Osmotic** (polyethylene glycol, lactulose, magnesium hydroxide): draw water into the lumen; fast, reliable onset.
**Stimulant** (senna, bisacodyl): directly stimulate enteric nerves/motility; reserve for short-term or breakthrough use.
**Secretagogues** (lubiprostone, linaclotide): increase intestinal chloride and fluid secretion; used for chronic constipation, IBS-C.
Polyethylene glycol 3350 — osmotic; first-line for chronic constipation.
Psyllium — bulk-forming. Senna — stimulant. Linaclotide — secretagogue.
Loperamide — antidiarrheal (peripheral opioid agonist).

Laxative mechanisms: bulk-forming holds water and expands stool; osmotic draws water into the lumen; stimulant activates enteric nerves; secretagogue increases chloride and fluid secretion → softer stool, faster transit.
**Loperamide — a peripheral opioid-receptor agonist that slows GI motility without significant CNS (opioid) effects at normal doses.**
Opioid brake on the gut: opioid agonist binds mu receptors on enteric neurons → less acetylcholine release → slower peristalsis, longer transit → more water absorbed, firmer stool.
Diphenoxylate/atropine — a combination opioid-receptor agonist; **atropine is included at a subtherapeutic dose specifically to discourage misuse/overdose**.
Bismuth subsalicylate — antisecretory, mild antimicrobial, and anti-inflammatory effects; also used for dyspepsia.
Opioid receptor antagonists (methylnaltrexone, naloxegol, naldemedine, alvimopan) block gut μ-receptors without entering the CNS, so analgesia is kept.
**PEG is first-line for chronic constipation**; magnesium laxatives need caution in CKD.

Onset (Figure 2, illustrative): osmotic ~2 h and stimulant ~8 h act fastest; secretagogue ~1 day; stool softener ~2 days and bulk-forming ~60 h take longest. **A patient who needs relief tonight is not a bulk-forming candidate.**
Stimulants cause cramping and are for short-term use. Lubiprostone causes nausea; linaclotide causes diarrhea.
Loperamide enters the CNS poorly (P-gp efflux), but **very high doses can cause cardiac toxicity (QT prolongation)**.
Bismuth subsalicylate: salicylate warning; can darken stool and tongue.
Mineral oil: aspiration causes lipid pneumonitis; long-term use impairs fat-soluble vitamin absorption.
Sodium phosphate purgatives risk electrolyte shifts and acute renal failure — avoid in frail, elderly or renal patients.

**Avoid antimotility agents (loperamide, diphenoxylate/atropine) in suspected infectious/inflammatory diarrhea (e.g., C. difficile, invasive bacterial infection) — can worsen outcomes by delaying toxin/pathogen clearance.** Also avoid in bloody or febrile diarrhea.

Bulk-forming agents need adequate fluids and are avoided in obstruction. Linaclotide: contraindicated in mechanical obstruction and in children under 2; secretagogues avoided in mechanical obstruction.
Diphenoxylate/atropine is **Schedule V**; avoided in young children (the slides give under 2 and under 6; the profile says under 6).
Antidiarrheals should not be used with bloody diarrhea, high fever, or systemic toxicity.
Psyllium: separate from other drugs by 2 hours.
Bisacodyl: do not crush; avoid with antacids or milk.
Loperamide has limited CNS entry because of P-gp efflux.
Senna works in 6–12 hours orally; bisacodyl in 6–10 hours orally and 30–60 minutes rectally.
Slowing transit in an infectious or inflammatory process can worsen the picture (toxic megacolon risk in C. difficile) — “stopping diarrhea” is not always the right first move.

Case: profuse watery diarrhea and fever three days after clindamycin. **Is loperamide an appropriate choice for symptomatic relief in this patient?** No — think C. difficile; avoid antimotility agents and treat the infection (oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin).

Why is atropine in Lomotil? At the tiny dose given it does nothing — but anyone taking big doses to get high gets unpleasant anticholinergic effects.
Why not loperamide in C. difficile? Slowing transit keeps toxin in the colon longer — toxic megacolon risk.

**Step therapy, escalating with disease severity:** 5-ASA agents for mild disease → short-term corticosteroids for flares → immunomodulators for maintenance → biologics/small molecules for moderate-to-severe disease.
This escalation ladder is the organizing framework for every IBD drug — ask where each drug “lives” on it.
Mesalamine — 5-ASA (step 1).
Prednisone, budesonide — corticosteroids (flares).
Azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine — immunomodulators (maintenance).
Infliximab, adalimumab, vedolizumab, ustekinumab, tofacitinib — targeted therapy.

**Mesalamine, sulfasalazine — anti-inflammatory action local to the GI mucosa.** Sulfasalazine reaches the colon → colonic bacteria cleave the azo bond → 5-ASA (mesalamine) plus sulfapyridine released → 5-ASA acts on mucosa, reducing inflammatory mediators → less mucosal inflammation.
Azathioprine is converted to 6-mercaptopurine → metabolized to thioguanine nucleotides → block purine synthesis in lymphocytes → fewer proliferating T and B cells → slow, sustained remission.

**Targeted therapy:** TNF-α inhibitors block tumor necrosis factor-alpha (infliximab, adalimumab); the integrin inhibitor blocks α4β7 integrin-mediated leukocyte gut-homing (vedolizumab); the IL-12/23 inhibitor blocks interleukin-12 and -23 signaling (ustekinumab); the JAK inhibitor blocks intracellular JAK signaling (tofacitinib).
Vedolizumab is the most **gut-selective** agent — less systemic immunosuppression than TNF inhibitors, JAK inhibitors, or thiopurines.
**Chemistry & formulations:** azo compounds (sulfasalazine, balsalazide, olsalazine) are cleaved by colonic bacteria; mesalamine formulations release 5-ASA at set pH or times.
5-ASA: first-line for mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis; more limited role in Crohn disease.
Corticosteroids: short-term induction of remission during an acute flare; not appropriate for long-term maintenance given cumulative toxicity.
Immunomodulators: long-term maintenance of remission; onset is slow (weeks to months) — not useful for acute flares.
Delayed-release forms target the ileum or colon; enemas and suppositories treat distal disease.
Corticosteroids: prednisone 40–60 mg/d for flares, tapered after response; rectal forms for distal disease; not for maintenance.
**The major safety theme across immunomodulators and biologics: immunosuppression → increased infection risk.**
Sulfasalazine: the sulfapyridine component causes most adverse effects — rash, hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, agranulocytosis, folate deficiency (give folic acid); caution in sulfa allergy.
Mesalamine: monitor renal function (interstitial nephritis). 5-ASA agents are generally well tolerated — a favorable long-term safety profile relative to steroids and immunomodulators.
Thiopurines: increased infection and lymphoma risk; monitor CBC and liver tests (bone marrow suppression, hepatotoxicity).
Up to 40% cannot tolerate therapeutic sulfasalazine doses; give 1 mg/d folic acid; reversible oligospermia.
Anti-TNF: TB reactivation — test before starting; antibodies to the drug reduce response; infliximab infusion reactions in up to 10%.
Tofacitinib: fourfold herpes zoster reactivation (vaccinate first); check lipids at 8 weeks.
Sulfasalazine: caution in sulfa allergy (sulfapyridine).
No azathioprine/6-MP with absent TPMT activity (low in 11%, absent in 0.3%).
**Allopurinol blocks thiopurine metabolism — reduce the thiopurine dose by about two-thirds to three-quarters**; febuxostat is avoided.
Ketoconazole (CYP3A4 inhibitor) raises budesonide exposure.
Budesonide has high first-pass metabolism — less systemic exposure than prednisone.
Thiopurines take a median 17 weeks to benefit; budesonide bioavailability about 10% (CYP3A4 inhibitors raise it).
**Test TPMT and NUDT15 before starting thiopurines; low activity raises myelosuppression risk.**
**Before biologics:** tuberculosis and hepatitis B/C screening; update vaccines, especially live vaccines, before starting; regular labs to catch cytopenias, hepatotoxicity, or infection early.
Infliximab and adalimumab are the same TNF-α inhibitors as the RA biologic DMARDs in Lecture 2 — same mechanism, same risk profile in a new organ system.
“Fast but not for the long term” (steroids) vs. “slow but sustainable” (immunomodulators) parallels the acute-vs-chronic gout framework.
Case: newly diagnosed mild UC asks why mesalamine, not a biologic. **How would you explain the step-therapy rationale to this patient?**

Therapy is matched to severity: mild disease responds to 5-ASA with a favorable safety profile; biologics are reserved for moderate-to-severe or refractory disease given cost, administration burden, and immunosuppression risks.
Name stems: -ximab chimeric (infliximab, anti-TNF-α); -umab human (adalimumab, ustekinumab); -zumab humanized (vedolizumab, α4β7 integrin).

More stems: -tinib kinase inhibitor (tofacitinib, JAK); -sone corticosteroid (prednisone, short-term induction); -tide peptide (linaclotide, GC-C agonist). 5-ASA agents, thiopurines and opioid antidiarrheals share no stem. A stem is a memory aid, not a rule.

Why is vedolizumab gut-selective? α4β7 integrin is the gut-homing address tag; block it and leukocytes can’t enter the bowel, while immunity elsewhere is spared.
Why give folic acid with sulfasalazine? Sulfapyridine causes folate deficiency.
**What patients take on their own can change how their medications work.** Ask one question about any vitamin: can it build up to toxic levels?

**Fat-soluble (A, D, E, K):** stored in adipose tissue and the liver; accumulate with excess intake — real toxicity risk; absorption depends on dietary fat and bile, impaired by fat-malabsorption conditions.
**Water-soluble (B-complex, C):** not significantly stored — excreted renally; toxicity is rare except at very high supplemental doses; deficiency develops more quickly without ongoing intake.

Figure 8 (illustrative storage/toxicity-risk index): vitamin A 85 and D 90 (fat-soluble) vs. C 10 and B-complex 8 (water-soluble). Vitamin D and A toxicity from OTC overuse are the clearest real examples.
Cyanocobalamin (B12), folic acid, vitamin D, phytonadione (K1), ferrous sulfate.
St. John’s wort, ginkgo biloba, fish oil — supplements with drug interactions.
**B12 absorption:** dietary B12 is bound to food protein → stomach acid and pepsin release it → free B12 binds intrinsic factor from parietal cells → the complex is absorbed in the terminal ileum.
Reduced vitamin K is recycled by VKORC1; **warfarin blocks VKORC1, so fewer active factors** — active vitamin K carboxylates clotting factors II, VII, IX, X — so fewer active factors.

**Two ways to lower warfarin’s effect:** dietary vitamin K opposes it pharmacodynamically (supports clotting factor synthesis); St. John’s wort induces CYP enzymes and speeds clearance — a pharmacokinetic interaction. **Result: lower INR and less anticoagulation.**
**Enteral nutrition** (oral or tube feeding) is preferred whenever the gut is functional — **“if the gut works, use it”**; lower infection/complication risk.

**Parenteral nutrition** is delivered intravenously, bypassing the GI tract entirely; reserved for a non-functional or inaccessible GI tract; requires close monitoring — electrolyte shifts, refeeding syndrome, catheter-related infection (the main parenteral risk).
Treat B12 deficiency with intramuscular or high-dose oral B12.
**Vitamin B12 deficiency:** megaloblastic anemia and neurologic symptoms/neuropathy that can become irreversible if treatment is delayed.
**Folate:** deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia; critical in pregnancy to prevent neural tube defects.

**Vitamin D:** deficiency impairs bone mineralization (rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults). **Vitamin K:** deficiency impairs synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, increasing bleeding risk.
**Iron:** deficiency causes microcytic anemia; absorption is enhanced by vitamin C and impaired by concurrent antacid or PPI use.

**Refeeding sequence in prolonged starvation:** carbohydrate feeding raises insulin → phosphate, potassium and magnesium shift into cells → dangerously low levels: heart, muscle and breathing problems.
St. John’s wort: avoid with SSRIs, transplant drugs, HIV protease inhibitors, oral contraceptives, warfarin.
**St. John’s Wort — CYP3A4 induction; reduces effectiveness of many drugs (warfarin, oral contraceptives, some antiretrovirals).**
**Ginkgo biloba and fish oil — can increase bleeding risk, especially combined with anticoagulants/antiplatelets.**
**At risk for B12 deficiency:** long-term PPI or H2 blocker use, metformin (impairs ileal uptake), bariatric surgery, older age, vegan diets.
St. John’s wort activates PXR, inducing CYP 3A4, 2C9, 1A2 and P-glycoprotein: lowers digoxin, birth control, cyclosporine, HIV drugs, warfarin; serotonin syndrome with antidepressants.
Garlic, ginkgo and ginseng have antiplatelet effects — avoid or monitor with anticoagulants and around surgery.
Coenzyme Q10 and melatonin may decrease warfarin’s effect; glucosamine may increase the INR.
Fat-soluble vitamin absorption depends on dietary fat and bile.
Monitor B12 in long-term PPI or metformin users.
**Keep vitamin K intake consistent rather than avoiding it.** Check INR when starting or stopping any supplement; stopping St. John’s wort can raise INR.
**Refeeding:** start feeding slowly in malnourished patients; check phosphate, potassium and magnesium daily at the start; give thiamine before feeding begins.
**Supplements are not held to the same FDA premarket efficacy/safety standards as prescription drugs — potency and purity can vary by product.**
Always ask patients specifically about supplement use — many don’t mention it unless asked; counsel them to disclose all supplement use to every prescriber and pharmacist.

Applying the whole GI & Nutrition toolkit: for each patient, name a first-line approach AND the single biggest safety concern to check before prescribing/counseling.
**1.** Acid-peptic disease and antiemetics are managed by targeting specific points along well-defined pathways (parietal cell secretion; the vomiting reflex).
**2.** PPIs are the most potent antisecretory agents, but long-term use carries real risks that warrant periodic reassessment.

**3.** IBD therapy follows a step-wise escalation matched to disease severity. **4.** Biologic agents share mechanisms and immunosuppression risk across organ systems. **5.** Nutrition and supplements are not inert.
Pharmacology is cumulative, not siloed by unit: biologic mechanisms (Lecture 2) and drug-metabolism/interaction concepts (Lecture 1) reappear here in a new organ system.
**Patient A — GERD symptoms, needs rapid occasional relief:** an antacid for occasional relief; an H2 blocker or PPI if frequent.
**Patient B — confirmed H. pylori, penicillin allergy:** bismuth quadruple therapy.
**Patient C — moderate-to-severe Crohn disease, inadequately controlled on azathioprine:** a biologic or small molecule such as an anti-TNF agent.
**Patient D — warfarin patient starting an herbal mood supplement:** counsel on St. John’s wort and check INR.
**Recall Q1:** PPIs block the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase proton pump itself — the final common pathway for gastrin, histamine, and acetylcholine — unlike H2RAs, which block only the histamine input.
**Recall Q2:** recent macrolide exposure raises clarithromycin-resistance concern, favoring bismuth quadruple therapy over standard clarithromycin-based triple therapy.
**Recall Q3:** aprepitant blocks NK1; ondansetron 5-HT3; meclizine H1/M1; metoclopramide D2.
**Recall Q4:** antimotility agents can worsen infectious/inflammatory diarrhea like C. difficile by delaying toxin clearance and slowing transit — toxic megacolon risk.
**Recall Q5–6:** vedolizumab blocks α4β7 gut-homing (most gut-selective); St. John’s Wort induces CYP3A4, increasing warfarin metabolism and lowering INR — a pharmacokinetic drug-herb interaction.

**Integrated case:** H. pylori + penicillin allergy + macrolide two months ago → bismuth quadruple therapy (allergy rules out amoxicillin triple therapy; macrolide exposure raises clarithromycin-resistance concern).
Her subtherapeutic INR is St. John’s Wort inducing CYP3A4 — stop the supplement (or adjust warfarin) with close INR monitoring.

4.notes:

Know: Osmotic (polyethylene glycol, lactulose, magnesium hydroxide) draws water into the lumen. Magnesium needs caution in CKD.

Know: Stimulant (senna, bisacodyl) activates enteric nerves. Short-term or breakthrough use. Cramping.

5.title: Laxatives: How Each Class Works
5.notes: Say: "Four buckets: bulk-forming, osmotic, stimulant, secretagogue. Sort any laxative name into one of them."

6.title: Laxative Onset of Action by Mechanism
6.notes:
Use this to connect mechanism to clinical choice: a patient who needs relief tonight is not a bulk-forming-laxative candidate, no matter how favorable its long-term safety profile is.

Instructor script:

Say: The values are illustrative onset times, not trial data.

7.notes: Quick check: pause for students to answer before revealing slide 8.

8.title: Answer
8.notes: Answer C: osmotic or stimulant for relief within hours.

9.title: Antidiarrheal Agents
9.notes:
The "avoid in infectious diarrhea" caution is one of the highest-yield safety points in this section — slowing transit in an infectious or inflammatory process can actually worsen the clinical picture (e.g., toxic megacolon risk in C. difficile).

Instructor script:

Know: Loperamide has limited CNS entry because of P-gp efflux. Very high doses can cause cardiac toxicity (QT prolongation).

Know: Diphenoxylate/atropine is Schedule V. Atropine is there at a low dose to discourage misuse. Avoid in children under 2.

Know: Bismuth subsalicylate: salicylate warning, can darken stool and tongue.

10.title: Loperamide and Diphenoxylate: Opioid Brake on the Gut
10.notes: Say: "Loperamide and diphenoxylate are opioid agonists. They bind mu receptors on enteric neurons, reduce acetylcholine release, slow peristalsis and give more time for water absorption."

11.title: Is an Antimotility Agent Safe Here?
11.notes:
Great opportunity to connect back to the antibiotic-associated-diarrhea concept and reinforce that "stopping diarrhea" is not always the correct first move.

Instructor script:

Case: Diarrhea and fever after clindamycin. Ask: "Is loperamide appropriate?" Answer: no, think C. difficile and treat the infection (oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin).

12.title: Quick Check
12.notes: Quick check: Atropine in diphenoxylate. Pause for students to answer before revealing slide 13.

13.title: Answer
13.notes: Answer B: it discourages overdose or misuse.

14.notes:
Section transition.

Step therapy. Match the drug to the severity: 5-ASA for mild, steroids for flares, immunomodulators for maintenance, biologics and small molecules for moderate to severe disease.

15.title: Step Therapy in Inflammatory Bowel Disease
15.notes:
This escalation ladder is the organizing framework for every drug class in this section — ask students where each drug they learn next "lives" on this ladder.

Instructor script:

Say: "Step therapy. Match the drug to the severity: 5-ASA for mild, steroids for flares, immunomodulators for maintenance, biologics and small molecules for moderate to severe disease."

16.title: Aminosalicylates (5-ASA Agents)
16.notes:
Know: Sulfapyridine causes most adverse effects: rash, hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, agranulocytosis, folate deficiency (give folic acid). Caution in sulfa allergy.

Know: Mesalamine: monitor renal function (interstitial nephritis).

Know: Delayed-release forms target the ileum or colon. Enemas and suppositories treat distal disease.

17.title: 5-ASA: Local Anti-Inflammatory Action
17.notes: Say: "Sulfasalazine reaches the colon. Bacteria cleave the azo bond and release 5-ASA and sulfapyridine. 5-ASA acts on the mucosa."

18.title: Corticosteroids and Immunomodulators
18.notes:
The "fast but not for long-term" vs. "slow but sustainable" contrast here directly parallels the acute-vs-chronic gout framework from Lecture 2 — point that out explicitly if students took that unit.

Instructor script:

Say: "Fast but not for the long term versus slow but sustainable." Budesonide has high first-pass metabolism, so less systemic exposure than prednisone.

19.title: Azathioprine and 6-MP: Purine Antimetabolites
19.notes:
Say: "Azathioprine becomes 6-mercaptopurine, then thioguanine nucleotides, which block purine synthesis in lymphocytes."

Know: Test TPMT and NUDT15 before starting. Low activity raises myelosuppression risk.

Know: Allopurinol blocks metabolism. Reduce the thiopurine dose by about two-thirds to three-quarters.

Know: Monitor CBC and liver tests. Onset takes weeks to months. Infection and lymphoma risk rise.

20.title: Biologic & Small-Molecule Agents in IBD
20.notes:
TNF-α inhibitors are a direct callback to the biologic DMARDs from Lecture 2 — the same generic drugs (infliximab, adalimumab) reappear here treating a different organ system through the same mechanism. The next slide shows this full set as a mechanism diagram.

Instructor script:

Know: Targets: TNF-alpha (infliximab, adalimumab), integrin (vedolizumab), IL-12/23 (ustekinumab), JAK (tofacitinib).

21.title: Biologic & Targeted Therapies in IBD: Where Each Class Acts
21.notes:
Have students sort each drug into its target before revealing labels — the s
ame exercise used for the DMARD figure in Lecture 2, now applied to a new organ system.

Instructor script:

Sort each drug into its target before revealing labels: TNF-alpha (infliximab, adalimumab), integrin (vedolizumab), IL-12/23 (ustekinumab), JAK (tofacitinib).

22.title: Quick Check
22.notes: Quick check: pause for students to answer before revealing slide 23.

23.title: Answer
23.notes: Answer C: vedolizumab is gut-selective because it blocks alpha4beta7 integrin.

24.title: IBD Therapy Safety: Immunosuppression
24.notes:
This is almost a direct repeat of the DMARD-safety slide from Lecture 2 — a deliberate, explicit callback to reinforce that "biologic" as a drug category carries this risk profile regardless of the organ system being treated.

Instructor script:

Safety: Screen for TB and hepatitis B and C before starting a biologic. Update vaccines, especially live vaccines, first. Monitor labs.

25.title: Matching Therapy to Disease Severity
25.notes:
A good patient-communication exercise (IO3.6) — have students practice explaining step therapy in plain language, not just reciting the drug ladder.

Instructor script:

Case: Mild ulcerative colitis starts with mesalamine, not a biologic.

26.title: Quick Check
26.notes: Quick check: pause for students to answer before revealing slide 27.

27.title: Answer
27.notes: Answer B: Crohn flare on azathioprine: add a short steroid course.

28.title: Drug Names Reveal the Class: Bowel Disorders and IBD
28.notes: Say: "-ximab chimeric, -umab human, -zumab humanized, -tinib kinase inhibitor, -sone corticosteroid, -tide peptide. 5-ASA agents, thiopurines and the opioid antidiarrheals share no stem."

29.notes:
Section transition.

Ask one question about any vitamin: can it build up to toxic levels?

30.title: Fat-Soluble vs. Water-Soluble Vitamins
30.notes:
This distinction is the organizing concept for the whole vitamin section — "can it accumulate to toxic levels" is the single most useful question to ask about any vitamin.

Instructor script:

Say: "Ask one question about any vitamin: can it build up to toxic levels? Fat-soluble A, D, E, K store and can accumulate. Water-soluble B and C are excreted."

31.title: Fat-Soluble vs. Water-Soluble Vitamins: Storage and Toxicity Risk
31.notes:
Vitamin D and A toxicity (from excessive supplementation) are the clearest clinical examples to cite here — both are seen in real practice from over-the-counter supplement overuse.

Instructor script:

Say: The figure values are illustrative.

32.title: Vitamin & Mineral Deficiency Syndromes
32.notes:
The B12/PPI link and the vitamin K/clotting-factor link are the two points most worth emphasizing, since both connect directly back to earlier drug classes in this very unit.

Instructor script:

Know: Deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and neuropathy that can become irreversible.

Know: Folate: neural tube defects in pregnancy. Vitamin D: rickets and osteomalacia. Vitamin K: factors II, VII, IX, X. Iron: microcytic anemia, absorption helped by vitamin C and hurt by antacids and PPIs.

33.title: Vitamin B12 Absorption: Where PPIs and Metformin Interfere
33.notes:
Say: "Dietary B12 is bound to protein. Stomach acid and pepsin release it. It binds intrinsic factor and is absorbed in the terminal ileum."

Know: PPIs and H2 blockers reduce acid. Metformin impairs ileal uptake. Bariatric surgery, older age and vegan diets add risk.

Know: Monitor B12 in long-term PPI or metformin users. Treat with intramuscular or high-dose oral B12.

34.title: Vitamin K and CYP3A4 Inducers: A Classic Drug-Nutrient Interaction
34.notes:
This figure ties the whole unit together: a dietary nutrient and an herbal supplement both working against the same drug, through two completely different mechanisms (pharmacodynamic antagonism vs. pharmacokinetic induction).

Instructor script:

Say: "Two different ways to lower warfarin's effect. Vitamin K opposes it pharmacodynamically. St. John's wort induces CYP enzymes and speeds clearance, a pharmacokinetic interaction."

35.title: Warfarin: Vitamin K Cycle and Herbal Interactions
35.notes:
Say: Warfarin blocks VKORC1, which recycles vitamin K.

Know: Keep vitamin K intake consistent. Do not tell patients to avoid it.

Know: Check INR when starting or stopping any supplement. Stopping St. John's wort can raise INR.

Know: St. John's wort also lowers oral contraceptive and some antiretroviral levels. Ginkgo and fish oil raise bleeding risk.

36.title: Quick Check
36.notes: Quick check: pause for students to answer before revealing slide 37.

37.title: Answer
37.notes: Answer A: decreased anticoagulant effect from CYP induction.

38.title: Enteral & Parenteral Nutrition: The Basics
38.notes:
The "if the gut works, use it" principle is a simple, memorable rule students can apply across many clinical contexts — worth stating explicitly as the single takeaway from this slide.

Instructor script:

Say: "If the gut works, use it."

39.title: Choosing the Nutrition Route and Avoiding Refeeding Syndrome
39.notes:
Say: Refeeding: carbohydrate raises insulin, phosphate, potassium and magnesium shift into cells, and levels fall dangerously.

Know: Start slowly in malnourished patients. Check phosphate, potassium and magnesium daily at first. Give thiamine before feeding. Catheter infection is the main parenteral risk.

40.title: Herbal & Dietary Supplement Safety Counseling
40.notes:
This slide operationalizes IO3.6 (patient communication/safety) directly — the counseling point about "ask specifically" is something students can apply in every future patient encounter, not just GI/nutrition cases.

Instructor script:

Say: Supplements are not held to premarket efficacy or safety standards. Always ask specifically. Have patients tell every prescriber and pharmacist.

41.title: The Supplement No One Asked About
41.notes:
This case is the direct clinical application of Figure 10 — a great closing vignette for the nutrition section.

Instructor script:

Case: Subtherapeutic INR after starting St. John's wort.

45.title: Which Drug Would You Choose?
45.notes:
Have students work in pairs: for each patient, name a first-line approach AND the single biggest safety concern to check before prescribing/counseling.

Instructor script:

Suggested answers: A, an antacid for occasional relief or an H2 blocker or PPI if frequent. B, bismuth quadruple therapy. C, a biologic or small molecule such as an anti-TNF agent. D, counsel on St. John's wort and check INR.

46.title: Quick Check
46.notes: Quick check: Long-term PPI for GERD. Pause for students to answer before revealing slide 47.

47.title: Answer
47.notes: Answer B: reassess the need periodically.

54.title: Polyethylene glycol 3350 (MiraLAX)
54.notes:
Drug: Polyethylene glycol 3350 (MiraLAX)

Class: Osmotic laxative

Formulation: Powder for solution (17 g scoop); large-volume bowel-prep kits

Dose (adult): 17 g in 4-8 oz fluid PO once daily; OTC use up to 7 days

Indications: Chronic and occasional constipation; bowel preparation (higher volumes)

Adverse effects: Bloating, nausea, gas, loose stools

Contraindications: Bowel obstruction, perforation, ileus, toxic megacolon

Toxicity / overdose: Dehydration and electrolyte loss with excess or bowel-prep volumes; rare allergic reactions

55.title: Psyllium (Metamucil)
55.notes:
Drug: Psyllium (Metamucil)

Class: Bulk-forming laxative

Formulation: Powder, capsules, wafers

Dose (adult): About 3.4-6 g PO 1-3 times daily with at least 8 oz water

Indications: Constipation, IBS, mild cholesterol lowering

Adverse effects: Bloating, gas, abdominal fullness

Contraindications: Bowel obstruction, fecal impaction, dysphagia

Toxicity / overdose: Esophageal or intestinal obstruction if taken with too little fluid; allergy; separate from other drugs by 2 hours

56.title: Methylcellulose (Citrucel)
56.notes:
Drug: Methylcellulose (Citrucel)

Class: Bulk-forming laxative

Formulation: Powder; caplets 500 mg

Dose (adult): About 2 g PO in 8 oz water 1-3 times daily; onset 12-72 hours

Indications: Constipation, stool bulking

Adverse effects: Bloating, gas

Contraindications: Bowel obstruction, dysphagia

Toxicity / overdose: Obstruction if taken without adequate fluid; may slow absorption of other drugs

57.title: Lactulose
57.notes:
Drug: Lactulose

Class: Osmotic laxative, ammonia-lowering agent

Formulation: Oral solution 10 g/15 mL

Dose (adult): Constipation: 15-30 mL PO daily; hepatic encephalopathy: 30-45 mL PO 3-4 times daily, titrated to 2-3 soft stools

Indications: Constipation, hepatic encephalopathy

Adverse effects: Gas, bloating, cramps, diarrhea

Contraindications: Galactosemia, bowel obstruction

Toxicity / overdose: Dehydration and hypernatremia with over-use; worsens diabetes control slightly

58.title: Senna (Senokot)
58.notes:
Drug: Senna (Senokot)

Class: Stimulant laxative

Formulation: Tablet 8.6 mg sennosides; liquid

Dose (adult): 8.6-17.2 mg PO at bedtime (max 34 mg/day); onset 6-12 hours

Indications: Short-term constipation, opioid-induced constipation

Adverse effects: Cramping, diarrhea, urine discoloration, melanosis coli

Contraindications: Bowel obstruction, appendicitis, undiagnosed abdominal pain

Toxicity / overdose: Hypokalemia and dehydration with chronic use; laxative dependence

59.title: Bisacodyl (Dulcolax)
59.notes:
Drug: Bisacodyl (Dulcolax)

Class: Stimulant laxative

Formulation: DR tablet 5 mg; suppository 10 mg

Dose (adult): 5-15 mg PO at bedtime; 10 mg PR once daily; PO onset 6-12 hours, PR 15-60 min

Indications: Constipation, bowel preparation

Adverse effects: Cramping, nausea, rectal irritation

Contraindications: Bowel obstruction, appendicitis, acute abdomen

Toxicity / overdose: Do not crush; avoid with antacids or milk; excess causes diarrhea, hypokalemia

60.title: Lubiprostone (Amitiza)
60.notes:
Drug: Lubiprostone (Amitiza)

Class: Chloride channel (ClC-2) activator

Formulation: Capsule 8/24 mcg

Dose (adult): Chronic constipation: 24 mcg PO BID with food; IBS-C (women): 8 mcg BID

Indications: Chronic idiopathic constipation, IBS-C, opioid-induced constipation

Adverse effects: Nausea, diarrhea, headache, abdominal pain

Contraindications: Mechanical GI obstruction

Toxicity / overdose: Dizziness, syncope or dyspnea (rare); overdose: nausea, diarrhea; avoid in pregnancy unless needed

61.title: Linaclotide (Linzess)
61.notes:
Drug: Linaclotide (Linzess)

Class: Guanylate cyclase-C agonist

Formulation: Capsule 72/145/290 mcg

Dose (adult): CIC: 72-145 mcg PO daily; IBS-C: 290 mcg daily; 30 minutes before the first meal

Indications: Chronic idiopathic constipation, IBS-C

Adverse effects: Diarrhea, abdominal pain, gas, bloating

Contraindications: Boxed: children under 2 years; mechanical GI obstruction

Toxicity / overdose: Severe dehydration (deaths in young children); severe diarrhea; stop if severe or prolonged

62.title: Loperamide (Imodium)
62.notes:
Drug: Loperamide (Imodium)

Class: Peripheral mu-opioid agonist

Formulation: Capsule 2 mg; tablet 2 mg; oral liquid

Dose (adult): 4 mg PO first dose, then 2 mg after each loose stool; max 16 mg/day Rx, 8 mg/day OTC

Indications: Acute and chronic diarrhea, traveler's diarrhea

Adverse effects: Constipation, cramps, dizziness, nausea

Contraindications: Bloody stool or high fever, C. difficile, children under 2, ileus

Toxicity / overdose: High doses: QT prolongation, torsades, cardiac arrest; CNS depression in overdose (naloxone, repeated)

63.title: Diphenoxylate/atropine (Lomotil)
63.notes:
Drug: Diphenoxylate/atropine (Lomotil)

Class: Opioid antidiarrheal (C-V) plus anticholinergic

Formulation: Tablet 2.5 mg/0.025 mg; oral liquid 2.5 mg/5 mL

Dose (adult): 5 mg (2 tablets) PO QID initially; max 20 mg/day; reduce as controlled

Indications: Adjunct for diarrhea

Adverse effects: Drowsiness, dry mouth, tachycardia, urinary retention

Contraindications: Children under 6 years, obstructive jaundice, C. difficile or infectious diarrhea

Toxicity / overdose: Respiratory depression (especially children) and anticholinergic toxicity; naloxone, with monitoring for relapse

64.title: Mesalamine (Lialda, Asacol HD, Pentasa)
64.notes:
Drug: Mesalamine (Lialda, Asacol HD, Pentasa)

Class: 5-ASA aminosalicylate

Formulation: DR tablet 800 mg/1.2 g; capsule; suppository 1,000 mg; enema 4 g/60 mL

Dose (adult): Mild-moderate UC: 2.4-4.8 g/day PO once daily or divided; 1,000 mg PR at bedtime for proctitis

Indications: Induction and maintenance in ulcerative colitis; mild Crohn disease (some forms)

Adverse effects: Headache, nausea, abdominal pain, flatulence

Contraindications: Salicylate hypersensitivity

Toxicity / overdose: Interstitial nephritis (monitor creatinine); acute intolerance syndrome (cramps, bloody diarrhea); he

65.title: Sulfasalazine (Azulfidine)
65.notes:
Drug: Sulfasalazine (Azulfidine)

Class: Sulfapyridine plus 5-ASA prodrug

Formulation: Tablet 500 mg; EN-tabs DR 500 mg

Dose (adult): Active UC: start 1-2 g/day, titrate to 3-4 g/day in divided doses; maintenance 2 g/day; folic acid 1 mg daily

Indications: Ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis (EN-tabs)

Adverse effects: Nausea, headache, rash, orange urine, reversible low sperm count

Contraindications: Sulfa or salicylate allergy, intestinal or urinary obstruction, porphyria

Toxicity / overdose: Agranulocytosis, hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, hepatitis; folate

66.title: Budesonide (Entocort EC, Uceris)
66.notes:
Drug: Budesonide (Entocort EC, Uceris)

Class: Locally acting corticosteroid

Formulation: Capsule 3 mg; ER tablet 9 mg; foam

Dose (adult): Crohn disease: 9 mg PO every morning for up to 8 weeks; UC: 9 mg ER tablet daily for 8 weeks

Indications: Mild-moderate ileocecal Crohn disease, mild-moderate UC

Adverse effects: Headache, nausea, acne, adrenal suppression with long courses

Contraindications: Hypersensitivity

Toxicity / overdose: Hypercortisolism with CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, grapefruit juice); infection risk

67.title: Prednisone
67.notes:
Drug: Prednisone

Class: Systemic corticosteroid

Formulation: Tablet 1/2.5/5/10/20/50 mg; oral solution

Dose (adult): Flare: 40-60 mg PO daily, then taper over weeks; short-term induction only

Indications: Induction of remission in IBD flares; many inflammatory conditions

Adverse effects: Hyperglycemia, insomnia, mood change, weight gain, infection risk

Contraindications: Systemic fungal infection; live vaccines at high dose

Toxicity / overdose: Adrenal suppression and adrenal crisis on abrupt stopping; osteoporosis, cataracts, Cushingoid features

68.title: Azathioprine (Imuran)
68.notes:
Drug: Azathioprine (Imuran)

Class: Purine antimetabolite

Formulation: Tablet 50/75/100 mg; IV

Dose (adult): IBD maintenance: 1.5-2.5 mg/kg PO daily after TPMT/NUDT15 testing; onset 8-12 weeks

Indications: Maintenance of remission in Crohn disease and UC (off-label), organ transplant

Adverse effects: Nausea, leukopenia, hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, infection

Contraindications: Hypersensitivity; prior alkylating therapy; use with febuxostat

Toxicity / overdose: Myelosuppression (higher with low TPMT), lymphoma and hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma; allopurinol requires major dose cut

69.title: Mercaptopurine (6-MP, Purinethol)
69.notes:
Drug: Mercaptopurine (6-MP, Purinethol)

Class: Purine antimetabolite

Formulation: Tablet 50 mg; oral suspension

Dose (adult): IBD (off-label): 1-1.5 mg/kg PO daily after TPMT/NUDT15 testing

Indications: Maintenance in Crohn disease and UC; acute lymphoblastic leukemia

Adverse effects: Nausea, leukopenia, hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis

Contraindications: Hypersensitivity; use with febuxostat

Toxicity / overdose: Myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity, lymphoma risk; reduce dose with allopurinol

70.title: Infliximab (Remicade)
70.notes:
Drug: Infliximab (Remicade)

Class: Chimeric anti-TNF-alpha antibody

Formulation: IV 100 mg vial; SC 120 mg syringe (Zymfentra)

Dose (adult): Induction 5 mg/kg IV at weeks 0, 2, 6, then every 8 weeks; dose may be escalated

Indications: Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis

Adverse effects: Infusion reactions, headache, infections, rash

Contraindications: Hypersensitivity to murine proteins; high doses in moderate-severe heart failure

Toxicity / overdose: TB and hepatitis B reactivation, serious infections, demyelination, hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma; anti-dr

71.title: Adalimumab (Humira)
71.notes:
Drug: Adalimumab (Humira)

Class: Human anti-TNF-alpha antibody

Formulation: SC pen or syringe 40 mg/0.4 mL

Dose (adult): Crohn disease and UC: 160 mg SC day 1, 80 mg day 15, then 40 mg every 2 weeks

Indications: Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis

Adverse effects: Injection-site reactions, infections, headache, rash

Contraindications: Hypersensitivity; active serious infection

Toxicity / overdose: TB and hepatitis B reactivation, serious infections, malignancy, demyelination, lupus-like syndrome

72.title: Vedolizumab (Entyvio)
72.notes:
Drug: Vedolizumab (Entyvio)

Class: Humanized alpha4beta7 integrin antibody

Formulation: IV 300 mg vial; SC pen 108 mg

Dose (adult): 300 mg IV at weeks 0, 2, 6, then every 8 weeks; SC 108 mg every 2 weeks after IV induction

Indications: Moderate-severe ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease

Adverse effects: Nasopharyngitis, headache, arthralgia, infusion reactions

Contraindications: Hypersensitivity

Toxicity / overdose: Infections and rare liver injury; PML not reported to date but vigilance advised; gut-selective with less systemic immunosuppression

73.title: Ustekinumab (Stelara)
73.notes:
Drug: Ustekinumab (Stelara)

Class: Human anti-IL-12/23 antibody

Formulation: IV 130 mg/26 mL vial; SC 45/90 mg

Dose (adult): IV induction by weight (260 mg under 55 kg, 390 mg 55-85 kg, 520 mg over 85 kg), then 90 mg SC every 8 weeks

Indications: Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, psoriasis

Adverse effects: Nasopharyngitis, injection-site reactions, headache, fatigue

Contraindications: Hypersensitivity

Toxicity / overdose: Serious infections, TB, reversible posterior leukoencephalopathy (rare), hypersensitivity

74.title: Tofacitinib (Xeljanz)
74.notes:
Drug: Tofacitinib (Xeljanz)

Class: JAK inhibitor

Formulation: Tablet 5/10 mg; XR tablet 11/22 mg

Dose (adult): UC: 10 mg PO BID for at least 8 weeks, then 5 mg BID (lowest effective dose)

Indications: Ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis

Adverse effects: Headache, nasopharyngitis, raised lipids, herpes zoster

Contraindications: Hypersensitivity; severe hepatic impairment; active serious infection

Toxicity / overdose: Boxed: serious infections, mortality, malignancy, MACE, thrombosis; cytopenias, GI perforation; use after TNF-inhibitor failure

75.title: Warfarin (Coumadin, Jantoven)
75.notes:
Drug: Warfarin (Coumadin, Jantoven)

Class: Vitamin K antagonist (VKORC1 inhibitor)

Formulation: Tablet 1/2/2.5/3/4/5/6/7.5/10 mg

Dose (adult): Start 2-5 mg PO daily, adjust to INR goal (usually 2-3)

Indications: Venous thromboembolism, atrial fibrillation, mechanical heart valves

Adverse effects: Bleeding, bruising, hair loss, skin necrosis (rare)

Contraindications: Pregnancy (most cases), active bleeding, recent CNS surgery, uncontrolled hypertension

Toxicity / overdose: Hemorrhage; reversal with vitamin K and 4-factor PCC; many interactions (St. John's wort lowers INR)

76.title: Cyanocobalamin (vitamin B12)
76.notes:
Drug: Cyanocobalamin (vitamin B12)

Class: Vitamin

Formulation: Tablet 100-1,000 mcg; IM injection 1,000 mcg/mL; nasal gel

Dose (adult): Deficiency: 1,000 mcg IM daily for 1 week, then weekly, then monthly; or 1,000-2,000 mcg PO daily

Indications: B12 deficiency, pernicious anemia, PPI or metformin-related deficiency

Adverse effects: Injection-site pain, mild diarrhea, itching; early low potassium when treating severe anemia

Contraindications: Cobalt allergy, Leber hereditary optic neuropathy

Toxicity / overdose: Low toxicity; excess is excreted; folate alone can mask B12 anemia while ne

77.title: Folic acid (vitamin B9)
77.notes:
Drug: Folic acid (vitamin B9)

Class: Water-soluble vitamin

Formulation: Tablet 0.4/0.8/1 mg; injection

Dose (adult): Deficiency 1 mg PO daily; 0.4 mg daily for neural tube defect prevention (4 mg if prior NTD)

Indications: Megaloblastic anemia, pregnancy, sulfasalazine and methotrexate therapy

Adverse effects: Nausea, bloating, rash (rare)

Contraindications: Untreated B12 deficiency (can mask anemia)

Toxicity / overdose: Low toxicity; high doses may mask B12 deficiency and worsen neurologic injury

78.notes:
Drug: Vitamin D (cholecalciferol)

Class: Fat-soluble vitamin

Formulation: Capsule/tablet 400-5,000 IU; 50,000 IU capsule

Dose (adult): Maintenance 600-800 IU PO daily; deficiency 50,000 IU weekly for about 8 weeks

Indications: Rickets, osteomalacia, osteoporosis support, deficiency

Adverse effects: Usually none; nausea and constipation with excess

79.title: Phytonadione (vitamin K1)
79.notes:
Drug: Phytonadione (vitamin K1)

Class: Fat-soluble vitamin

Formulation: Tablet 5 mg; injection 10 mg/mL

Dose (adult): Warfarin over-anticoagulation: 1-10 mg PO or slow IV by INR; newborn prophylaxis 0.5-1 mg IM

Indications: Warfarin reversal, vitamin K deficiency bleeding, malabsorption

Adverse effects: Injection-site reactions; flushing

Contraindications: Hypersensitivity

Toxicity / overdose: IV: boxed warning for anaphylaxis (infuse slowly); overcorrection causes warfarin resistance

80.title: Ferrous sulfate
80.notes:
Drug: Ferrous sulfate

Class: Iron supplement

Formulation: Tablet 325 mg (65 mg elemental); liquid

Dose (adult): 325 mg PO once daily or every other day, ideally with vitamin C

Indications: Iron-deficiency anemia

Adverse effects: Constipation, nausea, dark stools, abdominal pain

Contraindications: Hemochromatosis, hemosiderosis, hemolytic anemia

Toxicity / overdose: Acute iron overdose is a pediatric emergency: GI bleeding, shock, liver failure; chelate with deferoxamine

81.title: St. John's wort (Hypericum perforatum)
81.notes:
Drug: St. John's wort (Hypericum perforatum)

Class: Herbal supplement (CYP/P-gp inducer)

Formulation: Capsule/tablet 300 mg (0.3% hypericin); tea

Dose (adult): Commonly 300 mg PO TID; not FDA-approved for treatment

Indications: Self-treated mild depression (limited evidence)

Adverse effects: Photosensitivity, GI upset, dizziness, dry mouth

Contraindications: With SSRIs, transplant drugs, HIV protease inhibitors, oral contraceptives, warfarin

Toxicity / overdose: Serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs; lowers levels of warfarin, cyclosporine, contraceptives

82.title: Ginkgo biloba
82.notes:
Drug: Ginkgo biloba

Class: Herbal supplement

Formulation: Capsule/tablet 40-120 mg

Dose (adult): 120-240 mg/day PO in divided doses; not FDA-approved for treatment

Indications: Self-treated memory complaints (limited evidence)

Adverse effects: Headache, GI upset, dizziness

Contraindications: Bleeding disorders; stop before surgery

U3-R11.question: Describe the step-wise escalation of IBD therapy, from first-line through biologic/small-molecule agents. Which biologic agent is relatively gut-selective rather than broadly immunosuppressive, and why?

U3-S.question:
A patient with confirmed H. pylori infection reports a penicillin allergy. Chart review shows she received a macrolide antibiotic for a respiratory infection two months ago. Separately, this same patient has been stable on warfarin for atrial fibrillation and mentions she started a St. John's Wort supplement for her mood three weeks ago, and her last INR came back subtherapeutic.
Which H. pylori eradication regimen is most appropriate here, and what two features of her history rule out the standard first-line regimen?
What explains her subtherapeutic INR, and what should happen with the St. John's Wort and her warfarin dosing going forward?

children.name: Class
facts: **Opposite problems, each with its own family of mechanisms.** Four laxative buckets: bulk-forming, osmotic, stimulant, secretagogue — sort any laxative name into one of them.
**Bulk-forming** (psyllium, methylcellulose): absorb water, increase stool bulk and transit; slowest onset; generally safest for long-term use.
**Osmotic** (polyethylene glycol, lactulose, magnesium hydroxide): draw water into the lumen; fast, reliable onset.
**Stimulant** (senna, bisacodyl): directly stimulate enteric nerves/motility; reserve for short-term or breakthrough use.
**Secretagogues** (lubiprostone, linaclotide): increase intestinal chloride and fluid secretion; used for chronic constipation, IBS-C.

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: Polyethylene glycol 3350 — osmotic; first-line for chronic constipation.
Psyllium — bulk-forming. Senna — stimulant. Linaclotide — secretagogue.
Loperamide — antidiarrheal (peripheral opioid agonist).

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: Laxative mechanisms: bulk-forming holds water and expands stool; osmotic draws water into the lumen; stimulant activates enteric nerves; secretagogue increases chloride and fluid secretion → softer stool, faster transit.
**Loperamide — a peripheral opioid-receptor agonist that slows GI motility without significant CNS (opioid) effects at normal doses.**
Opioid brake on the gut: opioid agonist binds mu receptors on enteric neurons → less acetylcholine release → slower peristalsis, longer transit → more water absorbed, firmer stool.
Diphenoxylate/atropine — a combination opioid-receptor agonist; **atropine is included at a subtherapeutic dose specifically to discourage misuse/overdose**.
Bismuth subsalicylate — antisecretory, mild antimicrobial, and anti-inflammatory effects; also used for dyspepsia.
Opioid receptor antagonists (methylnaltrexone, naloxegol, naldemedine, alvimopan) block gut μ-receptors without entering the CNS, so analgesia is kept.

children.name: Indications
facts: **PEG is first-line for chronic constipation**; magnesium laxatives need caution in CKD.

Onset (Figure 2, illustrative): osmotic ~2 h and stimulant ~8 h act fastest; secretagogue ~1 day; stool softener ~2 days and bulk-forming ~60 h take longest. **A patient who needs relief tonight is not a bulk-forming candidate.**

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: Stimulants cause cramping and are for short-term use. Lubiprostone causes nausea; linaclotide causes diarrhea.
Loperamide enters the CNS poorly (P-gp efflux), but **very high doses can cause cardiac toxicity (QT prolongation)**.
Bismuth subsalicylate: salicylate warning; can darken stool and tongue.
Mineral oil: aspiration causes lipid pneumonitis; long-term use impairs fat-soluble vitamin absorption.
Sodium phosphate purgatives risk electrolyte shifts and acute renal failure — avoid in frail, elderly or renal patients.

children.name: Contraindications
facts: **Avoid antimotility agents (loperamide, diphenoxylate/atropine) in suspected infectious/inflammatory diarrhea (e.g., C. difficile, invasive bacterial infection) — can worsen outcomes by delaying toxin/pathogen clearance.** Also avoid in bloody or febrile diarrhea.

Bulk-forming agents need adequate fluids and are avoided in obstruction. Linaclotide: contraindicated in mechanical obstruction and in children under 2; secretagogues avoided in mechanical obstruction.
Diphenoxylate/atropine is **Schedule V**; avoided in young children (the slides give under 2 and under 6; the profile says under 6).
Antidiarrheals should not be used with bloody diarrhea, high fever, or systemic toxicity.

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: Psyllium: separate from other drugs by 2 hours.
Bisacodyl: do not crush; avoid with antacids or milk.

children.name: Pharmacokinetics
facts: Loperamide has limited CNS entry because of P-gp efflux.
Senna works in 6–12 hours orally; bisacodyl in 6–10 hours orally and 30–60 minutes rectally.

children.name: Monitoring
facts: Slowing transit in an infectious or inflammatory process can worsen the picture (toxic megacolon risk in C. difficile) — “stopping diarrhea” is not always the right first move.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: Case: profuse watery diarrhea and fever three days after clindamycin. **Is loperamide an appropriate choice for symptomatic relief in this patient?** No — think C. difficile; avoid antimotility agents and treat the infection (oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin).

children.name: Class
facts: **Step therapy, escalating with disease severity:** 5-ASA agents for mild disease → short-term corticosteroids for flares → immunomodulators for maintenance → biologics/small molecules for moderate-to-severe disease.
This escalation ladder is the organizing framework for every IBD drug — ask where each drug “lives” on it.

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: Mesalamine — 5-ASA (step 1).
Prednisone, budesonide — corticosteroids (flares).
Azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine — immunomodulators (maintenance).
Infliximab, adalimumab, vedolizumab, ustekinumab, tofacitinib — targeted therapy.

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: **Mesalamine, sulfasalazine — anti-inflammatory action local to the GI mucosa.** Sulfasalazine reaches the colon → colonic bacteria cleave the azo bond → 5-ASA (mesalamine) plus sulfapyridine released → 5-ASA acts on mucosa, reducing inflammatory mediators → less mucosal inflammation.
Azathioprine is converted to 6-mercaptopurine → metabolized to thioguanine nucleotides → block purine synthesis in lymphocytes → fewer proliferating T and B cells → slow, sustained remission.

**Targeted therapy:** TNF-α inhibitors block tumor necrosis factor-alpha (infliximab, adalimumab); the integrin inhibitor blocks α4β7 integrin-mediated leukocyte gut-homing (vedolizumab); the IL-12/23 inhibitor blocks interleukin-12 and -23 signaling (ustekinumab); the JAK inhibitor blocks intracellular JAK signaling (tofacitinib).
Vedolizumab is the most **gut-selective** agent — less systemic immunosuppression than TNF inhibitors, JAK inhibitors, or thiopurines.
**Chemistry & formulations:** azo compounds (sulfasalazine, balsalazide, olsalazine) are cleaved by colonic bacteria; mesalamine formulations release 5-ASA at set pH or times.

children.name: Indications
facts: 5-ASA: first-line for mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis; more limited role in Crohn disease.
Corticosteroids: short-term induction of remission during an acute flare; not appropriate for long-term maintenance given cumulative toxicity.
Immunomodulators: long-term maintenance of remission; onset is slow (weeks to months) — not useful for acute flares.
Delayed-release forms target the ileum or colon; enemas and suppositories treat distal disease.
Corticosteroids: prednisone 40–60 mg/d for flares, tapered after response; rectal forms for distal disease; not for maintenance.

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: **The major safety theme across immunomodulators and biologics: immunosuppression → increased infection risk.**
Sulfasalazine: the sulfapyridine component causes most adverse effects — rash, hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, agranulocytosis, folate deficiency (give folic acid); caution in sulfa allergy.
Mesalamine: monitor renal function (interstitial nephritis). 5-ASA agents are generally well tolerated — a favorable long-term safety profile relative to steroids and immunomodulators.
Thiopurines: increased infection and lymphoma risk; monitor CBC and liver tests (bone marrow suppression, hepatotoxicity).
Up to 40% cannot tolerate therapeutic sulfasalazine doses; give 1 mg/d folic acid; reversible oligospermia.
Anti-TNF: TB reactivation — test before starting; antibodies to the drug reduce response; infliximab infusion reactions in up to 10%.
Tofacitinib: fourfold herpes zoster reactivation (vaccinate first); check lipids at 8 weeks.

children.name: Contraindications
facts: Sulfasalazine: caution in sulfa allergy (sulfapyridine).
No azathioprine/6-MP with absent TPMT activity (low in 11%, absent in 0.3%).

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: **Allopurinol blocks thiopurine metabolism — reduce the thiopurine dose by about two-thirds to three-quarters**; febuxostat is avoided.
Ketoconazole (CYP3A4 inhibitor) raises budesonide exposure.

children.name: Pharmacokinetics
facts: Budesonide has high first-pass metabolism — less systemic exposure than prednisone.
Thiopurines take a median 17 weeks to benefit; budesonide bioavailability about 10% (CYP3A4 inhibitors raise it).

children.name: Monitoring
facts: **Test TPMT and NUDT15 before starting thiopurines; low activity raises myelosuppression risk.**
**Before biologics:** tuberculosis and hepatitis B/C screening; update vaccines, especially live vaccines, before starting; regular labs to catch cytopenias, hepatotoxicity, or infection early.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: Infliximab and adalimumab are the same TNF-α inhibitors as the RA biologic DMARDs in Lecture 2 — same mechanism, same risk profile in a new organ system.
“Fast but not for the long term” (steroids) vs. “slow but sustainable” (immunomodulators) parallels the acute-vs-chronic gout framework.
Case: newly diagnosed mild UC asks why mesalamine, not a biologic. **How would you explain the step-therapy rationale to this patient?**

Therapy is matched to severity: mild disease responds to 5-ASA with a favorable safety profile; biologics are reserved for moderate-to-severe or refractory disease given cost, administration burden, and immunosuppression risks.
Name stems: -ximab chimeric (infliximab, anti-TNF-α); -umab human (adalimumab, ustekinumab); -zumab humanized (vedolizumab, α4β7 integrin).

More stems: -tinib kinase inhibitor (tofacitinib, JAK); -sone corticosteroid (prednisone, short-term induction); -tide peptide (linaclotide, GC-C agonist). 5-ASA agents, thiopurines and opioid antidiarrheals share no stem. A stem is a memory aid, not a rule.

children.name: Class
facts: **What patients take on their own can change how their medications work.** Ask one question about any vitamin: can it build up to toxic levels?

**Fat-soluble (A, D, E, K):** stored in adipose tissue and the liver; accumulate with excess intake — real toxicity risk; absorption depends on dietary fat and bile, impaired by fat-malabsorption conditions.
**Water-soluble (B-complex, C):** not significantly stored — excreted renally; toxicity is rare except at very high supplemental doses; deficiency develops more quickly without ongoing intake.

Figure 8 (illustrative storage/toxicity-risk index): vitamin A 85 and D 90 (fat-soluble) vs. C 10 and B-complex 8 (water-soluble). Vitamin D and A toxicity from OTC overuse are the clearest real examples.

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: Cyanocobalamin (B12), folic acid, vitamin D, phytonadione (K1), ferrous sulfate.
St. John’s wort, ginkgo biloba, fish oil — supplements with drug interactions.

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: **B12 absorption:** dietary B12 is bound to food protein → stomach acid and pepsin release it → free B12 binds intrinsic factor from parietal cells → the complex is absorbed in the terminal ileum.
Reduced vitamin K is recycled by VKORC1; **warfarin blocks VKORC1, so fewer active factors** — active vitamin K carboxylates clotting factors II, VII, IX, X — so fewer active factors.

**Two ways to lower warfarin’s effect:** dietary vitamin K opposes it pharmacodynamically (supports clotting factor synthesis); St. John’s wort induces CYP enzymes and speeds clearance — a pharmacokinetic interaction. **Result: lower INR and less anticoagulation.**

children.name: Indications
facts: **Enteral nutrition** (oral or tube feeding) is preferred whenever the gut is functional — **“if the gut works, use it”**; lower infection/complication risk.

**Parenteral nutrition** is delivered intravenously, bypassing the GI tract entirely; reserved for a non-functional or inaccessible GI tract; requires close monitoring — electrolyte shifts, refeeding syndrome, catheter-related infection (the main parenteral risk).
Treat B12 deficiency with intramuscular or high-dose oral B12.

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: **Vitamin B12 deficiency:** megaloblastic anemia and neurologic symptoms/neuropathy that can become irreversible if treatment is delayed.
**Folate:** deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia; critical in pregnancy to prevent neural tube defects.

**Vitamin D:** deficiency impairs bone mineralization (rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults). **Vitamin K:** deficiency impairs synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, increasing bleeding risk.
**Iron:** deficiency causes microcytic anemia; absorption is enhanced by vitamin C and impaired by concurrent antacid or PPI use.

**Refeeding sequence in prolonged starvation:** carbohydrate feeding raises insulin → phosphate, potassium and magnesium shift into cells → dangerously low levels: heart, muscle and breathing problems.

children.name: Contraindications
facts: St. John’s wort: avoid with SSRIs, transplant drugs, HIV protease inhibitors, oral contraceptives, warfarin.

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: **St. John’s Wort — CYP3A4 induction; reduces effectiveness of many drugs (warfarin, oral contraceptives, some antiretrovirals).**
**Ginkgo biloba and fish oil — can increase bleeding risk, especially combined with anticoagulants/antiplatelets.**
**At risk for B12 deficiency:** long-term PPI or H2 blocker use, metformin (impairs ileal uptake), bariatric surgery, older age, vegan diets.
St. John’s wort activates PXR, inducing CYP 3A4, 2C9, 1A2 and P-glycoprotein: lowers digoxin, birth control, cyclosporine, HIV drugs, warfarin; serotonin syndrome with antidepressants.
Garlic, ginkgo and ginseng have antiplatelet effects — avoid or monitor with anticoagulants and around surgery.
Coenzyme Q10 and melatonin may decrease warfarin’s effect; glucosamine may increase the INR.

children.name: Pharmacokinetics
facts: Fat-soluble vitamin absorption depends on dietary fat and bile.

children.name: Monitoring
facts: Monitor B12 in long-term PPI or metformin users.
**Keep vitamin K intake consistent rather than avoiding it.** Check INR when starting or stopping any supplement; stopping St. John’s wort can raise INR.
**Refeeding:** start feeding slowly in malnourished patients; check phosphate, potassium and magnesium daily at the start; give thiamine before feeding begins.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: **Supplements are not held to the same FDA premarket efficacy/safety standards as prescription drugs — potency and purity can vary by product.**
Always ask patients specifically about supplement use — many don’t mention it unless asked; counsel them to disclose all supplement use to every prescriber and pharmacist.

Case: warfarin for atrial fibrillation, subtherapeutic INR despite adherence; started St. John’s Wort for mood three weeks ago. **How does this explain the subtherapeutic INR, and what should happen next?**
CYP3A4 induction speeds warfarin metabolism — asking about supplements is a required part of every medication reconciliation.
The B12/PPI link and the vitamin K/clotting-factor link tie back to earlier drug classes in this unit.
Under DSHEA (1994), supplements are regulated as foods: the FDA must prove a product harmful before restricting it.

tree.name: Part 4 · Putting It All Together: GI & Nutrition Toolkit

children.name: Key definitions
facts: Applying the whole GI & Nutrition toolkit: for each patient, name a first-line approach AND the single biggest safety concern to check before prescribing/counseling.

children.name: How it works
facts: **1.** Acid-peptic disease and antiemetics are managed by targeting specific points along well-defined pathways (parietal cell secretion; the vomiting reflex).
**2.** PPIs are the most potent antisecretory agents, but long-term use carries real risks that warrant periodic reassessment.

**3.** IBD therapy follows a step-wise escalation matched to disease severity. **4.** Biologic agents share mechanisms and immunosuppression risk across organ systems. **5.** Nutrition and supplements are not inert.
Pharmacology is cumulative, not siloed by unit: biologic mechanisms (Lecture 2) and drug-metabolism/interaction concepts (Lecture 1) reappear here in a new organ system.

children.name: Clinical relevance
facts: **Patient A — GERD symptoms, needs rapid occasional relief:** an antacid for occasional relief; an H2 blocker or PPI if frequent.
**Patient B — confirmed H. pylori, penicillin allergy:** bismuth quadruple therapy.
**Patient C — moderate-to-severe Crohn disease, inadequately controlled on azathioprine:** a biologic or small molecule such as an anti-TNF agent.
**Patient D — warfarin patient starting an herbal mood supplement:** counsel on St. John’s wort and check INR.

children.name: Drugs named as examples
facts: **Recall Q1:** PPIs block the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase proton pump itself — the final common pathway for gastrin, histamine, and acetylcholine — unlike H2RAs, which block only the histamine input.
**Recall Q2:** recent macrolide exposure raises clarithromycin-resistance concern, favoring bismuth quadruple therapy over standard clarithromycin-based triple therapy.
**Recall Q3:** aprepitant blocks NK1; ondansetron 5-HT3; meclizine H1/M1; metoclopramide D2.
**Recall Q4:** antimotility agents can worsen infectious/inflammatory diarrhea like C. difficile by delaying toxin clearance and slowing transit — toxic megacolon risk.
**Recall Q5–6:** vedolizumab blocks α4β7 gut-homing (most gut-selective); St. John’s Wort induces CYP3A4, increasing warfarin metabolism and lowering INR — a pharmacokinetic drug-herb interaction.

children.name: Exam traps
facts: **Integrated case:** H. pylori + penicillin allergy + macrolide two months ago → bismuth quadruple therapy (allergy rules out amoxicillin triple therapy; macrolide exposure raises clarithromycin-resistance concern).
Her subtherapeutic INR is St. John’s Wort inducing CYP3A4 — stop the supplement (or adjust warfarin) with close INR monitoring.

hy: Four laxative buckets: bulk-forming (slowest, safest), osmotic (fast; PEG first-line), stimulant (short-term), secretagogue (IBS-C).
No antimotility agents in C. difficile or bloody/febrile diarrhea.
IBD therapy follows a step-wise escalation matched to disease severity — from 5-ASA agents to biologics/small molecules.
Biologic agents share both their targeted mechanisms and their immunosuppression-related safety profile across organ systems (RA in Lecture 2, IBD here).
TPMT/NUDT15 before thiopurines; allopurinol → cut dose by 2/3–3/4.
Nutrition and dietary supplements are not inert — vitamin status, drug-nutrient interactions, and herbal supplements can all meaningfully change drug therapy outcomes.
St. John’s wort induces CYP3A4 → warfarin cleared faster → lower INR.
Long-term PPI or metformin → check B12.
Refeeding: start slowly, check phosphate/potassium/magnesium, thiamine first.
